newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean groups donate 30,000 tonnes corn to North.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean groups donate 30,000 tonnes corn to North.

text.p: South Korean civic groups on Friday donated an additional 30,000 tonnes of corn to famine-threatened North Korea.
Seven religious and other civic groups said in a joint statement the supply would be on top of 50,000 tonnes of food being shipped to the communist state by the South Korean Red Cross.
"North Korea faces a dangerous situation where food stocks will run out by June-July without outside help," the statement said.
A spokesman of the groups said they would buy corn in China before shipping it to the North via the Red Cross, the only delivery channel allowed for the South Korean private sector.

Under an accord hammered out last month between the North and South Korean Red Cross societies, trains carrying the first shipments of the 50,000 tonnes of relief supplies arrived in the North on Thursday.
For the first time in 12 years, North Korea allowed South Korean Red Cross officials to visit the country to oversee the delivery.
The Red Cross last went to North Korea in 1985 to help South Koreans whose families had been divided by the 1950-53 Korean War to visit their relatives.

It was also the first time Pyongyang allowed southern officials to deliver food directly to the North since it appealed for international aid after floods in 1995 turned large tracts of the nation's breadbasket into a wasteland.
Previous relief supplies had been made through the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies.
North Korea, which was again hit by devastating floods last year, has admitted some of its children are starving.
The spokesman said the civic groups wanted the South Korean Red Cross to send the additional relief supplies by the end of July but transportation difficulties could delay the shipments.
The Red Cross has already promised to supply 50,000 tonnes of corn, flour, powdered milk and instant noodles by end-July.
International aid agencies have warned that North Korea desperately needs large-scale food aid to avert severe famine caused by years of economic decline and natural disasters.

South Korea, accusing North Korea of manipulating data to exaggerate its hunger and deprivation in a bid to secure international help, said it would not rush to help its Cold War rival until the North took action -- such as cutting military spending -- to solve its chronic food problems.
